paras: The disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson took place near Dawson, Georgia, in late November or early December 1881, when white men seized Thompson, a young Black man, as a suspect in an attack on a man named John E. Moreland and carried him away. He was reported beaten to death, but searchers found only a bloody shirt and socks buried in a swamp. A wire dispatch carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which headlined the robbery rather than the killing.

According to an account first printed in the Cincinnati Times, John Edward Moreland, who lived about six miles from Dawson on the road to Chickasawhatchee, left town about dark to return home. Near the outskirts of Dawson, he said, three men attacked him and tried to rob him, but he escaped. The wire dispatch from Dawson put it more strongly, saying that Moreland "was assaulted and robbed by three negroes."

Suspicion fell on Mark Thompson, whom the wire described as "supposed to be one of the robbers." White men captured him and, in the Cincinnati Times version, "carried away in a buggy" and "it is said beaten to death." In a swamp near Morehead's house, searchers found part of a shirt and a pair of socks "very much stained with blood," buried, and the ground for several feet around looked as if there had been "a severe scuffle". No trace of Thompson's body was found.

A correspondent of the Macon Telegraph and Messenger, quoted by the Savannah Morning News on December 1, wrote that Thompson had been "kidnapped and probably murdered by a party of white men" and that the matter was "to be fully investigated." No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no later report says whether Thompson was found.

The earliest report came from inside Georgia, where the Savannah Morning News ran the Macon correspondent's item in a column of state news; it called Thompson a kidnapping victim and said nothing of a robbery. The wire version, dated Dawson, December 2, reached the Salt Lake Herald, the Wheeling Register and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on December 3, filed among other crime items. Its headlines pointed at the alleged robbers: the Record-Union used "Robbed by Negroes—Beaten to Death," and the Eureka Daily Sentinel headed it "Murdered by Three Negroes," though the text said Moreland had only been assaulted and robbed.

Condensed versions dropped the wire's hedges. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said Thompson was "captured by a mob of white men and beaten to death," and the Maysville Daily Evening Bulletin called him "a negro highwayman" who was beaten to death and buried in a swamp. The St. Paul Daily Globe ran the brief on December 4 and again on December 5. On December 15 the Jonesborough Herald and Tribune reprinted the fuller Cincinnati Times account under the headline "A Highwayman's Fate," although its text called Thompson only "suspected."

The accounts differ on the date. The Macon correspondent placed the kidnapping in "the early part of last week" in an item printed December 1, while the wire, dated December 2, said the robbery happened "yesterday," and the Daily Globe said "Thursday." Because the Savannah item was already in print on December 1, the Georgia report is the better evidence that the seizure took place in late November. The accounts also differ on the alleged crime: the wire said Moreland was robbed, while the Cincinnati Times account said the robbery was only attempted and rested on Moreland's own word.

reader.title: Disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson
bases: White men seized Mark Thompson, a Black man suspected of a highway robbery, carried him off, and were reported to have beaten him to death, without any officer or legal process mentioned [A1][A4][A11].

Thompson was seized by 'a party of white men' (a 'mob' in one brief) as a suspected robber and was reported beaten to death, but every detailed account qualifies the death ('probably murdered', 'reported', 'it is said') and no body was found [A1][A4][A5][A11].

A Georgia correspondent's report (A1), the Dawson wire dispatch (A2, A4, A7) and the Cincinnati Times account (A11) independently agree that white men seized Thompson and probably killed him, though none confirms the death with a body.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Dawson dispatch as a one-paragraph crime item, with headlines that named the robbery rather than the killing ('Robbed by Negroes—Beaten to Death', 'Murdered by Three Negroes').
The Georgia report described a kidnapping and probable murder 'by a party of white men' and promised an investigation, without accusing Thompson of anything.
Condensed versions dropped the wire's hedges, stating flatly that Thompson was 'a negro highwayman' or was beaten to death by 'a mob of white men'.
